renalAdjustment: Use only when renal function and product labeling permit.
alternatives: Aminoglycoside single dose (gentamicin 5 mg/kg, tobramycin 5 mg/kg, amikacin or plazomicin 15 mg/kg IV once); gepotidacin 1.5 g PO every 12 hours; pivmecillinam 370 mg PO every 8 hours (IDSA dosing, differs from FDA label); sulopenem etzadroxil-probenecid 500 mg/500 mg PO every 12 hours; TMP-SMX 160 mg trimethoprim component every 12 hours — all are preferred options with no preferential order. Oral fosfomycin 3 g single dose is an alternative for ESBL-producing E. coli only.
notes: 2026 IDSA AMR preferred options are listed alphabetically and are not presented as a universal ranking. Use susceptibility and clinical context. Oral nitrofurantoin is not suggested as step-down therapy for ESBL-E bloodstream infection. Doses assume normal renal and hepatic function.

dose: 8–15 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component, divided (uncomplicated cystitis: 160 mg trimethoprim component every 12 hours)
alternatives: Ciprofloxacin (400 mg IV every 8 hours or 750 mg PO every 12 hours) or levofloxacin (750 mg every 24 hours) if susceptible; cefepime-enmetazobactam (2.5 g every 8 hours over 2 hours) or a carbapenem (ertapenem 1 g every 24 hours; meropenem; imipenem) when oral options cannot be used; IV fosfomycin (6 g every 8 hours over 1 hour), aminoglycoside, or piperacillin-tazobactam as alternatives (piperacillin-tazobactam only if not critically ill and no bacteremia).
notes: 2026 AMR guidance requires confirmed in-vitro susceptibility. Transition to an active oral agent may be appropriate when clinical criteria are met. Oral sulopenem is an alternative only after initial clinical improvement. Cefepime alone is not suggested for ESBL-E cUTI even if susceptible.
source: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance / IDSA 2025 cUTI Guideline

dose: 1–2 g per dose; 2 g preferred for obesity, CNS infection, ECMO, or CrCl ≥130 mL/min
route: IV (extended infusion over 3 hours if feasible)
duration: Individualize by infection syndrome and response
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Label adjustment: CrCl above 50 mL/min every 8 hours; 26–50 every 12 hours; 10–25 half dose every 12 hours; below 10 half dose every 24 hours.
alternatives: Ertapenem 1 g IV every 24 hours, or imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg every 6 hours (over 3 hours if feasible) or 1 g every 8 hours over 1 hour, when appropriate; imipenem or meropenem is preferred over ertapenem if critically ill or hypoalbuminemic; cefepime-enmetazobactam 2.5 g (2 g/0.5 g) every 8 hours over 2 hours has a defined role in selected ESBL-E infections.
notes: For invasive ESBL-E infections, carbapenem therapy remains an important preferred approach. Piperacillin-tazobactam and cefepime are not suggested for invasive ESBL-E infection even if susceptible. After clinical response, oral step-down to TMP-SMX or a fluoroquinolone may be considered if susceptible; nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin and amoxicillin-clavulanate are not suggested for bloodstream infection. Do not use susceptibility-independent empiric selection as a substitute for microbiology.

setting: Invasive infection caused by organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC production
organisms: Enterobacter cloacae complex; Klebsiella aerogenes; Citrobacter freundii; Hafnia alvei
dose: 2 g IV over 30 minutes as a loading dose, then 2 g infused over 3 hours
duration: Individualize by syndrome and clinical response
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Renal adjustment required when indicated.
alternatives: Carbapenem or other susceptibility-directed therapy when clinically appropriate. Non-beta-lactam agents (TMP-SMX, fluoroquinolones) are reasonable when susceptible and appropriate for the site.
notes: 2026 guidance does not suggest ceftriaxone/cefotaxime/ceftazidime for invasive infection in organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant AmpC production; piperacillin-tazobactam is also not suggested for invasive infection. Cefepime is preferred when the cefepime MIC is 8 µg/mL or lower and an ESBL gene has not been identified. In non-severe infection already improving on ceftriaxone with adequate source control, completing the course may be reasonable.

dose: KPC: ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g (2 g/0.5 g) every 8 h over 3 h; meropenem-vaborbactam 4 g (2 g/2 g) every 8 h over 3 h; imipenem-relebactam 1.25 g every 6 h over 30 min. NDM: aztreonam-avibactam 2.67 g load over 3 h then 2 g every 6 h over 3 h; cefiderocol 2 g every 8 h over 3 h (CrCl ≥120: every 6 h). OXA-48-like: ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g every 8 h over 3 h.
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Renal adjustment required when indicated.
alternatives: KPC-producing CRE: ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, or imipenem-relebactam. NDM-producing CRE: aztreonam-avibactam or cefiderocol. OXA-48-like CRE: ceftazidime-avibactam (meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem-relebactam are not suggested). Non-carbapenemase-producing CRE: select therapy according to carbapenem susceptibility and clinical status.
notes: CRE treatment must be selected according to carbapenemase mechanism, carbapenem susceptibility, infection site, and susceptibility testing. Combination therapy is not routinely suggested once an active beta-lactam has been identified.

dose: 2.67 g (2 g aztreonam/0.67 g avibactam) IV once over 3 hours as a loading dose, then 2 g (1.5 g/0.5 g) infused over 3 hours
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Renal adjustment required when indicated.
alternatives: Ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g every 8 hours plus aztreonam 2 g every 8 hours, each over 3 hours, given together by Y-site, if aztreonam-avibactam is unavailable. Eravacycline or tigecycline only for infections not involving the bloodstream or urinary tract.
notes: 2026 IDSA lists aztreonam-avibactam and cefiderocol (2 g every 8 hours over 3 hours; CrCl ≥120: every 6 hours) as preferred options for NDM-producing Enterobacterales, and preferentially suggests aztreonam-avibactam when available.

setting: Complicated UTI caused by DTR P. aeruginosa
dose: Ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g (2 g/0.5 g) every 8 h over 3 h; ceftolozane-tazobactam 3 g (2 g/1 g) every 8 h over 3 h; imipenem-relebactam 1.25 g every 6 h over 30 min; cefiderocol 2 g every 8 h over 3 h (CrCl ≥120: every 6 h)
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Renal adjustment required when indicated.
alternatives: Ceftolozane-tazobactam, imipenem-relebactam, and cefiderocol are equally preferred beta-lactam options (see notes); once-daily amikacin (15 mg/kg first dose) or tobramycin (7 mg/kg first dose) are alternatives, with later doses and interval set by pharmacokinetic evaluation.
notes: Cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam are ALL preferred options for DTR P. aeruginosa cUTI in the 2026 IDSA AMR guidance — listed alphabetically with no overall order of preference. (Cefiderocol drops to alternative-only status for non-urinary DTR Pseudomonas infection, not for cUTI.) For the rare uncomplicated UTI caused by DTR P. aeruginosa, the 2026 guidance points to the cUTI approach.

setting: Pneumonia or other infection outside urinary tract
dose: Ceftolozane-tazobactam 3 g (2 g/1 g) every 8 h over 3 h; ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g (2 g/0.5 g) every 8 h over 3 h; imipenem-relebactam 1.25 g every 6 h over 30 min; cefiderocol (alternative) 2 g every 8 h over 3 h
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Renal adjustment required when indicated.
alternatives: Ceftazidime-avibactam; imipenem-relebactam are preferred alternatives according to susceptibility. Cefiderocol is an alternative for non-urinary infection.
notes: For DTR P. aeruginosa infections outside the urinary tract, IDSA 2026 lists ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam as preferred options. For pneumonia, ceftolozane-tazobactam is preferred. Cefiderocol is an alternative. If a carbapenemase is identified: for KPC-producing P. aeruginosa, cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam and imipenem-relebactam are preferred; cefiderocol is preferred for NDM-producing isolates. Combination therapy is not suggested when in vitro susceptibility to an active beta-lactam is confirmed.

dose: Sulbactam-durlobactam 2 g (1 g/1 g) every 6 h over 3 h (CrCl ≥130: every 4 h) PLUS meropenem 1–2 g every 8 h over 3 h OR imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg every 6 h over 3 h (or 1 g every 8 h over 1 h)
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Renal adjustment required when indicated.
alternatives: If sulbactam-durlobactam is not immediately available: high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam (9 g sulbactam per day, either 9 g [6 g/3 g] every 8 h over 4 h or 27 g [18 g/9 g] continuous over 24 h) plus at least one other active agent, as bridge therapy only until sulbactam-durlobactam plus a carbapenem can start. If sulbactam-durlobactam resistance is present: two non-sulbactam active agents, or add sulbactam-durlobactam to cefiderocol.
notes: 2026 IDSA identifies sulbactam-durlobactam in combination with a carbapenem as the priority approach for invasive CRAB infection; alternative options are for bridge therapy only.

dose: Cefiderocol 2 g every 8 h over 3 h (CrCl ≥120: every 6 h); aztreonam-avibactam 2.67 g load over 3 h then 2 g every 6 h over 3 h
renalAdjustment: IDSA doses assume normal renal function. Agent-specific renal adjustment required when applicable.
alternatives: Aztreonam-avibactam, preferably in combination with a second active agent, is an alternative option.
notes: For invasive S. maltophilia infection, 2026 IDSA designates cefiderocol monotherapy as the preferred treatment. Treatment should be based on susceptibility and clinical assessment; distinguish infection from colonization.

setting: Clinically improving patient initially treated parenterally
dose: According to selected agent. IDSA 2026 AMR Table 1 oral examples (adult, normal renal function): ciprofloxacin 750 mg every 12 h; levofloxacin 750 mg every 24 h; TMP-SMX 8–15 mg/kg/day trimethoprim component divided every 8 to 12 h
duration: Usually complete the recommended short course
alternatives: Continue parenteral therapy when oral therapy is not effective, feasible or appropriate.
notes: IDSA 2025 suggests IV-to-oral transition when the patient is clinically improving, can take oral medication, and an effective oral option is available.

duration: 5–7 days for fluoroquinolone OR 7 days for non-fluoroquinolone in typical improving cases
alternatives: Individualize for subgroups excluded from trials or when clinical response/source control is inadequate.
notes: For cUTI with Gram-negative bacteremia and clinical improvement, IDSA suggests 7 days of effective therapy. Duration is counted from the first day of effective therapy.

duration: At least 5 days and until clinically stable (2019 ATS/IDSA). A 2025 ATS-only update — not IDSA-endorsed — suggests <5 days (minimum 3) once clinical stability is reached.
renalAdjustment: Adjust for renal function as appropriate.
alternatives: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg daily, or clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily) only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%.
notes: 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline is the only IDSA-endorsed version and remains CURRENT. ATS published a 2025 update independently after IDSA declined to co-sign it (dispute was over empiric antibiotics for virus-positive outpatients); that update also suggests no empiric antibiotics for outpatients without comorbidities who test positive for a respiratory virus. Treat 2025 changes as ATS guidance, not joint IDSA-endorsed guidance.

duration: At least 5 days and until clinically stable
alternatives: Beta-lactam alternatives, each with azithromycin 500 mg daily or clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily: ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5–3 g every 6 hours, cefotaxime 1–2 g every 8 hours, or ceftaroline 600 mg every 12 hours. Or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy: levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily. Beta-lactam plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily if both a macrolide and a fluoroquinolone are contraindicated.
notes: 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline remains the only IDSA-endorsed version and is current. A 2025 ATS-only update (not IDSA-endorsed) also addresses lung ultrasound as an imaging alternative and corticosteroid use in severe inpatient CAP — ATS guidance only, not jointly IDSA-endorsed.

duration: 5 days; extend if not clinically improved
renalAdjustment: Adjust for renal function when indicated.
alternatives: Penicillin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, dicloxacillin or clindamycin depending on clinical context.
notes: IDSA lists the 2014 SSTI guideline as CURRENT. Typical cellulitis without systemic signs needs an agent active against streptococci; MRSA coverage is usually unnecessary unless penetrating trauma, injection drug use, MRSA elsewhere, or systemic inflammatory signs are present.
source: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guideline 2014
